metadata.title: Znanje matematike in naravoslovja med osnovnošolci v Sloveniji in po svetu: Izsledki raziskave TIMSS 2011

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: TIMSS 2011 in this Slovenian report uses a stratified two-stage school/class sampling design, with schools randomly selected for the first part and a larger set of schools selected for the main study. For the main achievement estimates, students receive weights reflecting the proportion of the target population represented by each sampled student, accounting for stratification by region, school size, and school performance, and for nonresponse at the class level. The report explicitly states that national results are computed with weighting so that each student represents a number of students in the population, and that estimates therefore refer to the full population rather than only the sample. The report also describes the use of IDB Analyzer for correct computation of achievement scales and standard errors under the complex design; however, it does not provide the exact weight variable name(s) in the text.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report describes plausible values (five PVs) derived from an IRT-based model and that final statistics are computed as the average across the five PVs, but it does not document a specific missing-data procedure for questionnaire or item nonresponse at the student level. Because TIMSS uses complex sampling and PV-based scaling, missingness handling may be embedded in the IEA processing pipeline; the Slovenian report does not specify whether cases were excluded, imputed, or otherwise treated. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling details.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses TIMSS 2011 main study data for Slovenia, covering Grade 4 and Grade 8. It excludes students without parental consent and students with special-needs decisions where they could not meet minimum standards; it also excludes students who were physically unable to solve tasks without help. For the achievement analysis, it reports that 14 Grade 8 students and 29 Grade 4 students were excluded, and that the final test-taking numbers were 4492 Grade 4 students and 4415 Grade 8 students. For national results, all data are weighted to reflect the sampling design and population representation.

data.outcome_summary: This Slovenian TIMSS 2011 report documents international comparisons and trends in mathematics achievement for Grade 4 and Grade 8, using TIMSS’s IRT-based scaling and plausible values framework. Students solve one of 14 test booklets; achievement is modeled using item response theory and then summarized on a 0–1000 scale (mean 500, SD 100), with five plausible values used to compute final statistics. The report explains the two-stage stratified sampling of schools and classes under Statistics Canada’s sampling procedures, and it states that national estimates are produced with student weights reflecting each sampled student’s representation of the population. It also reports exclusion rules (no parental consent; certain special-needs cases; inability to complete tasks) and provides achievement benchmarks such as international averages and TIMSS proficiency “benchmarks” (e.g., 400/475/550/625 for Grade 4). No machine-learning predictive modeling is conducted; results are presented as descriptive and benchmark-based comparisons with standard errors and statistical significance criteria.
